entries.meaning: A round, firm fruit with red, green, or yellow skin and white flesh. ---
examples: I put an apple in her lunchbox every morning.
These apples came from the orchard down the road.
He ate half an apple and threw the rest away.

entries.meaning: A long curved tropical fruit with soft flesh and thick yellow skin. ---
examples: Slice a banana into your cereal.
The bananas went brown in three days.
She's allergic to bananas, so skip the smoothie.

entries.meaning: A round citrus fruit with thick skin and sweet juicy segments. ---
examples: I peeled an orange for the kids.
The oranges in this bag are seedless.
Fresh-squeezed orange juice costs twice as much.

entries.meaning: A sweet fruit that is narrow at the top and rounded at the bottom. ---
examples: That pear isn't ripe yet — give it two more days.
We poached the pears in red wine.
She packed a pear and a granola bar.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like pair and pare.

entries.meaning: A soft round fruit with fuzzy skin and a large pit. ---
examples: Georgia peaches show up around the end of June.
The peach was so juicy it ran down my arm.
I'll take a slice of peach pie.

entries.meaning: A small smooth-skinned fruit with sweet flesh and a single pit. ---
examples: The plums are on sale this week.
He bit into a plum and made a face.
These plums are better cooked than raw.

entries.meaning: A small round fruit that grows in bunches on a vine. ---
examples: The kids finished a whole bag of grapes.
Don't give whole grapes to a toddler.
One grape rolled under the table.

entries.meaning: A small round red fruit with a pit and a long stem. ---
examples: We picked cherries until our hands were purple.
There's one cherry left on top of the sundae.
Cherries don't stay good for long.

entries.meaning: A soft red fruit with tiny seeds on the outside. ---
examples: The strawberries at the farmers market are worth the drive.
She dipped a strawberry in melted chocolate.
I'm making strawberry shortcake for Sunday.

entries.meaning: A small dark blue berry that grows on a bush. ---
examples: Add a cup of blueberries to the batter.
I froze the blueberries so they'd last.
He picked a blueberry off the top of his pancake.

entries.meaning: A soft red berry made up of many tiny sections. ---
examples: Raspberries get moldy almost overnight.
There's a raspberry stain on your shirt.
We planted raspberries along the back fence.
entries.contrast: The p is silent: RAZ-beh-ree, never 'rasp-berry'.

entries.meaning: A dark purple-black berry that grows on a thorny bush. ---
examples: Wild blackberries grow all along that trail.
She got scratched reaching for a blackberry.
The blackberries turned the pie almost black.

entries.meaning: A yellow citrus fruit with very sour juice. ---
examples: Squeeze half a lemon over the fish.
The lemons were the size of softballs.
Can I get water with lemon?

entries.meaning: A small green citrus fruit with sour juice. ---
examples: Every taco stand puts a lime wedge on the plate.
We ran out of limes halfway through the party.
Roll the lime before you cut it and you'll get more juice.

entries.meaning: A large yellow or pink citrus fruit with a slightly bitter taste. ---
examples: He eats half a grapefruit every morning.
Grapefruit interferes with some medications.
These grapefruits are pink all the way through.

entries.meaning: A large tropical fruit with rough skin and sweet yellow flesh. ---
examples: The pineapple was still green at the top.
Grilled pineapple is better than it sounds.
We bought two pineapples for the party.

entries.meaning: A very large green fruit with sweet red flesh and black seeds. ---
examples: Nothing beats cold watermelon in August.
He carried the watermelon out to the car.
The watermelons were stacked up by the door.

entries.meaning: A large round fruit with a thick skin and sweet soft flesh. ---
examples: Cut the melon into cubes.
The melons weren't ripe yet.
She had melon and yogurt for breakfast.

entries.meaning: A melon with rough netted skin and orange flesh. ---
examples: A ripe cantaloupe smells sweet at the stem end.
We ate half the cantaloupe standing at the counter.
The cantaloupes were two for five dollars.

entries.meaning: A small orange fruit with soft flesh and a single pit. ---
examples: Dried apricots keep for months.
She spread apricot jam on her toast.
One apricot isn't much of a snack.
entries.contrast: Americans say AP-rih-kaht; the British say AY-prih-kot.

entries.meaning: A peach-like fruit with smooth skin instead of fuzz. ---
examples: A nectarine is basically a peach without the fuzz.
The nectarines were dripping ripe.
He packed a nectarine in his bag.

entries.meaning: A small brown fuzzy fruit with green flesh and tiny black seeds. ---
examples: Cut the kiwi in half and eat it with a spoon.
Kiwis are cheaper than they used to be.
The kiwi was too sour to finish.

entries.meaning: A tropical fruit with orange flesh and dark seeds in the center. ---
examples: Squeeze lime over the papaya.
Papayas ripen fast on the counter.
I'd never tried papaya before that trip.

entries.meaning: A round red fruit full of juicy seeds in white membrane. ---
examples: Getting the seeds out of a pomegranate is a project.
Pomegranate juice stains everything.
She bought two pomegranates for the salad.

entries.meaning: A soft sweet fruit with many tiny seeds inside. ---
examples: Fresh figs are only around for a few weeks.
He ate a fig right off the tree.
Dried figs are good with sharp cheese.

entries.meaning: A very sweet sticky brown fruit that grows on a palm tree. ---
examples: Dates are sweet enough to use instead of sugar.
She stuffed each date with an almond.
There's a bag of dates in the pantry.
entries.contrast: Spelled and pronounced exactly like date 'calendar day' — only context separates them.

entries.meaning: A dried grape. ---
examples: Pick the raisins out if you don't like them.
There's one raisin stuck to the bottom of the box.
Raisins are just dried grapes.

entries.meaning: A dried plum. ---
examples: My grandfather ate prunes every morning.
A prune is just a dried plum.
The recipe calls for chopped prunes.

entries.meaning: A small hard red berry with a very tart taste. ---
examples: Cranberries are too tart to eat raw.
We make the cranberry sauce from scratch.
She dropped a cranberry into her glass.

entries.meaning: A large tropical nut with a hard shell, white flesh, and liquid inside. ---
examples: He cracked the coconut open on the driveway.
The cake had shredded coconut on top.
Coconuts wash up on the beach here.

entries.meaning: A small soft round fruit with seeds and no pit. ---
examples: Don't eat any berry you can't identify.
The berries were gone by mid-July.
She topped the oatmeal with fresh berries.
entries.contrast: In General American, berry sounds the same as bury.

entries.meaning: A very small red, black, or white berry used in jams and baking. ---
examples: Black currants are hard to find in US stores.
The scone had exactly one currant in it.
Currants make a good jam.
entries.contrast: Homophone of current (an electric current; the current situation).

entries.meaning: A small citrus fruit with loose skin that peels off easily. ---
examples: He peeled a tangerine in one piece.
Tangerines show up in stores around the holidays.
The tangerine was much easier to peel than the orange.

entries.meaning: A plant with thick red stalks that are cooked and sweetened like fruit. ---
examples: Rhubarb is far too sour to eat on its own.
She grows rhubarb along the back fence.
Strawberry and rhubarb pie is the whole reason for summer.

entries.meaning: A sweet tropical fruit with pink or white flesh and small seeds. ---
examples: Guava juice is on every menu down there.
He brought back a whole bag of guavas.
The guava smelled ripe from across the room.

entries.meaning: A large starchy relative of the banana that is cooked before eating. ---
examples: Fried plantains came with every plate.
A plantain looks like a banana but has to be cooked.
She sliced the plantain thin and fried it in oil.
entries.contrast: Two syllables in American English: PLAN-tun, not 'plan-TAIN'.

entries.meaning: A long orange root vegetable that grows underground. ---
examples: She fed the horse a carrot.
Chop the carrots into coins.
There's one sad carrot left in the drawer.

entries.meaning: A round vegetable made of tightly packed green or purple leaves. ---
examples: Shred the cabbage for the slaw.
The cabbages were the size of basketballs.
Cabbage keeps in the fridge for weeks.

entries.meaning: A leafy green vegetable eaten raw in salads and sandwiches. ---
examples: The lettuce went limp in the bag.
Put some lettuce and tomato on it.
They grow lettuces in the greenhouse all winter.
entries.contrast: Sounds like 'let us' run together: LEH-tus, with no stress on the second syllable.

entries.meaning: A dark green leafy vegetable eaten raw or cooked. ---
examples: Spinach cooks down to almost nothing.
You've got spinach in your teeth.
I threw a handful of spinach into the smoothie.

entries.meaning: A green vegetable with a thick stalk and dense flowering heads. ---
examples: The kids will eat broccoli if there's cheese on it.
Steam the broccoli for about four minutes.
Half the broccoli went straight into the trash.

entries.meaning: A vegetable with a large white head of tightly packed flower buds. ---
examples: Cauliflower rice is not rice.
Roast the whole cauliflower at 425.
The cauliflowers were on sale two for one.

entries.meaning: A long green vegetable with watery flesh, usually eaten raw. ---
examples: Slice the cucumber as thin as you can.
Cucumbers from the garden taste completely different.
He put cucumber in the water pitcher.

entries.meaning: A vegetable with long pale green stalks eaten raw or in soups. ---
examples: Celery is basically crunchy water.
Chop two stalks of celery into the pot.
She dipped the celery in peanut butter.

entries.meaning: A fungus with a stem and a rounded cap, many kinds of which are eaten. ---
examples: Sauté the mushrooms until they brown.
Don't pick a mushroom unless you know what it is.
He picked the mushrooms off his pizza.

entries.meaning: A large dark purple vegetable with soft white flesh. ---
examples: Salt the eggplant first to draw out the water.
Eggplants bruise easily, so handle them gently.
She grilled the eggplant in thick slices.
entries.contrast: British English calls this an aubergine.

entries.meaning: A small round red root vegetable with a sharp peppery taste. ---
examples: Radishes add a little bite to the salad.
He ate a radish with butter and salt.
The radishes came up in three weeks.

entries.meaning: A round dark red root vegetable with an earthy sweet taste. ---
examples: Roasted beets turn everything on the plate pink.
She grated a raw beet into the salad.
Beets taste like dirt to some people.
entries.contrast: Homophone of beat. British English says beetroot for the vegetable.

entries.meaning: A round white and purple root vegetable with a slightly bitter taste. ---
examples: Turnips store well through the winter.
Mash the turnip in with the potatoes.
He'd never cooked a turnip before that night.

entries.meaning: Any of several thick-skinned vegetables from the gourd family. ---
examples: Butternut squash soup is on the menu all fall.
The squash took forty minutes to roast.
Squashes keep for months in a cool basement.

entries.meaning: A large round orange squash used for pies and Halloween carving. ---
examples: We carved the pumpkin the night before.
Pumpkin pie is the only reason for November.
The pumpkins were rotting on the porch.

entries.meaning: A vegetable with thin green spears eaten cooked. ---
examples: Snap the woody ends off the asparagus.
Asparagus is only really good in the spring.
He grilled the asparagus with olive oil and salt.

entries.meaning: A vegetable with tough overlapping leaves and a soft edible center. ---
examples: Eating a whole artichoke takes patience.
The artichokes were the size of grapefruit.
She put marinated artichoke hearts on the pizza.

entries.meaning: A dark green leafy vegetable with tough curly leaves. ---
examples: Massage the kale before you dress it.
Kale chips are surprisingly good.
He grows kale well into December.

entries.meaning: A vegetable like a large mild onion with a long white stem. ---
examples: Rinse the leeks well — they hold a lot of grit.
Potato and leek soup is about as easy as it gets.
Slice the white part of the leek and discard the rest.
entries.contrast: Homophone of leak.

entries.meaning: A young onion with a small white bulb and long green leaves. ---
examples: Sprinkle chopped scallions over the top.
Use the green part of the scallion too.
Scallions keep growing if you stand them in water.
entries.contrast: Also called a green onion in the US; British English says spring onion.

entries.meaning: A small mild onion that grows in a cluster of bulbs. ---
examples: One shallot, minced fine.
Shallots are milder than regular onions.
The vinaigrette is just oil, vinegar, and shallot.

entries.meaning: A pale root vegetable that looks like a carrot and tastes sweeter. ---
examples: Parsnips get sweeter after a frost.
Roast the parsnips along with the carrots.
That's not a white carrot, it's a parsnip.

entries.meaning: A starchy root vegetable with sweet orange or white flesh. ---
examples: Candied yams show up at every Thanksgiving.
She baked a yam for lunch.
Most yams sold in US stores are actually sweet potatoes.

entries.meaning: A green ridged pod eaten as a vegetable, especially in Southern cooking. ---
examples: Okra gets slimy if you cook it wrong.
Fried okra is a Southern staple.
She threw a handful of okra into the gumbo.

entries.meaning: A salad green with a sharp peppery flavor. ---
examples: Arugula has a peppery bite to it.
Toss the arugula with lemon juice and olive oil.
He picked the arugula off his pizza.
entries.contrast: British English calls this rocket.

entries.meaning: A young shoot from a seed, often eaten raw. ---
examples: Add the bean sprouts at the very end.
A single sprout had pushed through the soil.
The sprouts went bad after two days in the fridge.

entries.meaning: A round pale bean used in hummus, stews, and salads. ---
examples: Hummus is just chickpeas, tahini, and lemon.
Drain the chickpeas but save the liquid.
One chickpea rolled off the cutting board.

entries.meaning: A bean grown for oil, animal feed, and foods like tofu. ---
examples: Soybeans are the biggest crop in this county.
The whole field was planted in soybeans.
Tofu is made from soybeans.

entries.meaning: A plant that grows in the sea, some kinds of which are eaten. ---
examples: The rice was wrapped in seaweed.
Seaweed salad comes with the lunch special.
Dried seaweed keeps forever in the pantry.

entries.meaning: A herb with soft green leaves and a sweet, slightly peppery smell. ---
examples: Tear the basil — don't chop it.
The basil on the porch died in one cold night.
Tomato, mozzarella, and basil, and that's it.
entries.contrast: Americans say BAY-zul; the British say BAZ-ul.

entries.meaning: A herb with flat or curly green leaves used fresh in cooking. ---
examples: Parsley is more than a garnish.
Chop a handful of parsley over the top.
The parsley wilted in the bag on the way home.

entries.meaning: A herb with a strong cool taste, or a small candy flavored with it. ---
examples: There's mint growing all over the yard.
He put a sprig of mint in the iced tea.
She keeps mints in her purse.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
entries.contrast: Uncountable as the plant or flavor (some mint), countable as the candy (two mints).

entries.meaning: The fresh green leaves of the coriander plant, used in cooking. ---
examples: Some people think cilantro tastes like soap.
Hold the cilantro on mine, please.
She threw a handful of cilantro into the salsa.
entries.contrast: American English for the fresh leaves; the British call them coriander.

entries.meaning: A herb with tiny leaves and a strong earthy smell. ---
examples: Add a few sprigs of thyme to the pot.
The chicken was roasted with lemon and thyme.
Thyme dries better than most herbs.
entries.contrast: Homophone of time — the h is silent and the y is a long I.

entries.meaning: A herb with stiff needle-like leaves and a piney smell. ---
examples: Rosemary grows into a whole bush out here.
She rubbed the lamb with garlic and rosemary.
A little rosemary goes a long way.

entries.meaning: A herb with soft gray-green leaves and a strong savory taste. ---
examples: Brown the butter with a few leaves of sage.
The stuffing needs more sage.
Sage has a fuzzy gray-green leaf you can spot anywhere.

entries.meaning: A herb with small strong-smelling leaves, used dried in Italian cooking. ---
examples: Sprinkle dried oregano over the sauce.
Oregano is what makes it taste like pizza.
She keeps oregano and basil right by the stove.
entries.contrast: Americans stress the second syllable, uh-REH-guh-noh; the British say or-ih-GAH-noh.

entries.meaning: A herb with feathery leaves used with fish, potatoes, and pickles. ---
examples: Dill goes in almost every pickle recipe.
He chopped dill into the yogurt sauce.
The dill went to seed in the heat.

entries.meaning: A thin hollow green leaf with a mild onion taste, usually used chopped. ---
examples: Snip some chives over the eggs.
Chives come back every spring on their own.
There's a single chive laid across the top as garnish.

entries.meaning: A knobby root with a hot spicy taste, used fresh or dried. ---
examples: Grate a little fresh ginger into the sauce.
Ginger settles my stomach.
The recipe calls for ground ginger, not fresh.

entries.meaning: A very expensive yellow spice made from the threads of a crocus flower. ---
examples: Saffron costs more per ounce than gold.
A pinch of saffron turns the whole pot yellow.
She brought back real saffron from Spain.

entries.meaning: A sweet flavoring made from the dried pods of a tropical orchid. ---
examples: Use real vanilla, not the imitation kind.
A teaspoon of vanilla goes in at the very end.
Vanilla comes from an orchid, believe it or not.

entries.meaning: A hard brown seed grated as a warm sweet spice. ---
examples: Grate a little nutmeg over the eggnog.
Whole nutmegs hold their flavor much longer than ground.
Too much nutmeg will ruin the whole thing.

entries.meaning: A bright yellow spice made from a root, common in curry. ---
examples: Turmeric will stain your cutting board yellow.
Add a teaspoon of turmeric to the rice.
She takes turmeric for her joints.
entries.contrast: The first r is often dropped in speech: TOO-muh-rik is as common as TUR-muh-rik.

entries.meaning: A small oval seed in a thin shell, eaten roasted or made into butter. ---
examples: Peanuts aren't really nuts — they're legumes.
The flight attendant handed out peanuts.
He shelled a peanut and ate it.

entries.meaning: A nut with a wrinkled kernel inside a hard round shell. ---
examples: Toast the walnuts before you add them.
There's a walnut tree in the back yard.
Walnuts go rancid if you leave them out.

entries.meaning: A flat oval nut with a light brown skin and a mild sweet taste. ---
examples: A handful of almonds holds me until lunch.
Almond milk is in the cooler section.
She dropped an almond into the batter by accident.
entries.contrast: The l is silent: AH-mund.

entries.meaning: A curved, kidney-shaped nut with a soft, buttery texture. ---
examples: Cashews are the first thing gone from the mixed nuts.
He roasted the cashews with a little salt.
There was one cashew left in the jar.

entries.meaning: A long nut with a smooth shell, grown mostly in the southern US. ---
examples: Pecan pie is the whole point of Thanksgiving.
The pecans fall all over the driveway in October.
She toasted a cup of pecans for the salad.
entries.contrast: US pronunciations vary: pih-KAHN is most common, but PEE-kan is widespread in the South.

entries.meaning: A small round nut with a hard shell and a sweet, toasty flavor. ---
examples: That spread is mostly sugar and hazelnuts.
He ordered a hazelnut latte.
Crack the hazelnut and rub the skin off.

entries.meaning: A small green nut sold in a shell that splits open on one side. ---
examples: Pistachios are worth the effort.
She ate a whole bag of pistachios watching the game.
One pistachio wouldn't open at all.

entries.meaning: A large glossy brown nut that is roasted or boiled before eating. ---
examples: Roasted chestnuts smell like winter.
Score each chestnut before you roast it.
Chestnuts are starchy rather than oily like other nuts.
entries.contrast: The t of chest is silent: CHES-nut.

entries.meaning: The nut of an oak tree, sitting in a small rough cup. ---
examples: The squirrels buried acorns all over the lawn.
An acorn hit the roof and woke me up.
The acorns were thick under the old oak.

entries.meaning: The small hard part of a plant from which a new plant grows. ---
examples: Save the seeds and plant them next spring.
There's a seed stuck in my teeth.
Sunflower seeds are the standard dugout snack.

entries.meaning: A tall plant with a large yellow flower and edible seeds. ---
examples: The sunflowers were taller than the fence.
She planted a row of sunflowers along the driveway.
Sunflower oil has almost no flavor of its own.

entries.meaning: A plant whose small flat seeds are used on bread and pressed for oil. ---
examples: Sprinkle sesame seeds on top before baking.
The dressing is soy sauce and sesame oil.
Sesame burns fast, so watch the pan.

entries.meaning: The soft edible part inside a nut, or a single grain of corn or wheat. ---
examples: A few kernels never pop.
Cut the kernels off the cob with a sharp knife.
One popcorn kernel got stuck in my tooth.
entries.contrast: Homophone of colonel.

entries.meaning: A grain grown for food and animal feed, usually eaten as oatmeal. ---
examples: Steel-cut oats take longer but taste better.
He eats oats every single morning.
Oat milk froths better than almond.

entries.meaning: A grain used in soups, animal feed, and brewing beer. ---
examples: Barley makes the soup thick and filling.
Most barley around here goes to the breweries.
Add a half cup of pearl barley.

entries.meaning: The part of a plant that grows underground and takes in water. ---
examples: The plant's roots had filled the whole pot.
Ginger root keeps for weeks in the freezer.
He pulled the weed out by the root.

entries.meaning: The thin part of a plant that supports leaves, flowers, or fruit. ---
examples: Cut the stems at an angle.
Pull the stem off the strawberry first.
The stems are tougher than the leaves.

entries.meaning: The outer skin of a fruit or vegetable. ---
examples: Don't throw out the lemon peel — zest it first.
He slipped on a banana peel, which I thought only happened in cartoons.
Compost the peels instead of trashing them.

entries.meaning: The thick hard outer layer of some fruits, vegetables, or cheeses. ---
examples: Cut the rind off the watermelon.
Save the parmesan rind for soup.
The rinds all went into the compost.

entries.meaning: The single hard seed in the middle of a peach, cherry, or similar fruit. ---
examples: Watch out for the pit in the middle.
She spit the cherry pits into a napkin.
Remove the pit before you blend it.
entries.contrast: American English for the hard seed; British English says stone.

entries.meaning: The hard central part of a fruit that holds the seeds. ---
examples: Cut around the core of the apple.
He tossed the core out the car window.
The cores go in the compost bin.

entries.meaning: The main thick stem of a plant, or one long piece of celery or rhubarb. ---
examples: Trim the ends off the celery stalks.
One stalk of celery has almost no calories.
The corn stalks were taller than the barn.
entries.contrast: The l is silent: STAWK.

entries.meaning: A plant with a long climbing or trailing stem, such as a grape plant. ---
examples: The tomatoes ripened on the vine.
Vines had grown right over the fence.
He trained the vine up a trellis.

entries.meaning: A piece of land planted with fruit trees. ---
examples: We drove out to the apple orchard on Saturday.
The orchards bloom in late April.
Her family has run that orchard for sixty years.

entries.meaning: The gathering of a crop, or the amount gathered. ---
examples: The harvest came in early this year.
Two bad harvests in a row nearly ruined them.
Everybody works straight through the harvest.

entries.meaning: A plant grown in large amounts for food, or the amount produced in a season.
examples: Corn is the biggest crop in the state.
The crops need rain badly.
They rotate crops to keep the soil healthy.
